https://www.thetimes.com/world/us-world/.subtitle: Brian Niccol will travel from California to Seattle. Greenpeace have already criticised it as an ‘unjustifiable perk’
https://www.thetimes.com/world/us-world/.text:
When three twentysomething graduates named their new Seattle coffee venture after Starbuck, the steadfast first mate in Moby Dick, they could hardly have guessed that its future boss would gain notoriety for an epic voyage of his own — to the office.
Starbucks revealed this week that its new chief executive would not only be commuting the 1,000 miles from his home in Newport, California, to the company’s headquarters in Seattle, but he would be doing so by private jet.
When Brian Niccol, 50, joins next month he will not have to relocate to the state of Washington, where 4,000 Starbucks staff are based, but will instead be allowed to join the millions of Americans now enjoying “work from home” privileges.
The commute seemed to critics incompatible with the company’s 2020 pledge to reduce its carbon emissions by half over the next decade.
A Starbucks representative told CNBC that Niccol, who helped revive the Mexican food chain Chipotle after a series of poisoning incidents, will be expected to work from the Seattle office at least three days a week, in line with its hybrid work policies.
“Brian’s primary office and a majority of his time will be spent in our Seattle Support Center or out visiting customers and employees in our stores, and offices around the world,” the spokesman told The Times.
The business will set up a small remote office in Newport Beach for Niccol to use when working from California. He is also believed to have successfully negotiated a similar deal with his previous company.
“Going to need a lot more paper straws for this one,” joked one user on X, a reference to Starbucks’ introduction of sustainable straws to reduce landfill waste.
“If this man is commuting regularly on a private jet, do not let @Starbucks convince you they are environmentally conscious,” wrote another.
Others were more forgiving, pointing out the warmer climate in California was more favourable than the wetter Seattle weather. One X user wrote: “It’s jammy, but if you can swing it, why would you not?!”
Environmental scientists and climate activists were critical, however.
“As the world faces unprecedented heat waves, droughts, floods and other dire consequences of an accelerating climate crisis, it is unjustifiable for companies to offer company aircraft as employee perks,” Clara Thompson, a campaigner at Greenpeace, said.
“These jets are a stark symbol of social and climate injustice, where a privileged few indulge in the most environmentally damaging form of travel for mere convenience.”
According to the terms of his offer, Niccol’s annual base pay will be $1.6 million. On top of that he could get a performance-related bonus of as much as $7.2 million, and up to $23 million a year in Starbucks shares.
The announcement came as the coffee chain looks to boost flagging sales.
Niccol began his career in brand management at Procter and Gamble. He rose to executive level at Pizza Hut and later Taco Bell before leaving to join Chipotle in 2018. While in the role, the fast food chain’s sales doubled and its shares surged from less than $7 each to more than $50. His net worth is estimated at $60 million.

In a 2019 interview, he spoke about the importance of a work-life balance and revealed how much he valued the time he spent with his wife, Jennifer, and their three children.
Most companies still prefer their executives to maintain a primary residence near their headquarters, though there have been notable exceptions.
Victoria’s Secret has made a concession in allowing its new chief executive, Hillary Super, to be based at the retailer’s New York City offices, rather than at the company’s headquarters near Columbus, Ohio. David Calhoun, who headed up Boeing, started working from home when he took over before the pandemic and never relocated close to its main base in Arlington, Virginia.
Dan Coatsworth, an investment analyst at AJ Bell, said using a private jet would also send a bad message to customers and staff, and would not be a “practical way to run a $105 billion business” with about 400,000 employees.
“A leader needs to be at the heart of a business,” he said, “not sitting on the beach enjoying the perks of the job.”
Andrew Trull, a Starbucks spokesman, said in an emailed statement on Thursday: “Brian’s schedule will meet or exceed the hybrid work guidelines and workplace expectations we have for all partners, which sees employees required to work from the Seattle office at least three times a week.”
